title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, I won’t.
In this analysis, I look at total commuters across counties in Rhode Island, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably. I think the state’s small geographic size and proximity to Boston provides an interesting layer to commuter patterns.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Choosing what to measure

my_state <- "RI"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B08303_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Pulling the data

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

Let’s look at what came back.

dim(county_data)

[1] 5 5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  GEOID NAME                            variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                           <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 44001 Bristol County, Rhode Island    B08303_001    22071   703
2 44003 Kent County, Rhode Island       B08303_001    79144  1590
3 44005 Newport County, Rhode Island    B08303_001    37266   948
4 44007 Providence County, Rhode Island B08303_001   285849  4075

There are five counties in the state of Rhode Island, which matches the row count.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe/estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  NAME                            estimate   moe moe_pct
  <chr>                              <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Bristol County, Rhode Island       22071   703    3.19
2 Newport County, Rhode Island       37266   948    2.54
3 Washington County, Rhode Island    57178  1424    2.49
4 Kent County, Rhode Island          79144  1590    2.01
5 Providence County, Rhode Island   285849  4075    1.43


Bristol County has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate. Its margin of error percentage is 3.185%.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 2  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 3 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence     1
2 Low confidence      1
3 Moderate            3


1 county falls into high confidence, 1 falls into low confidence, and the remaining 3 fall into moderate confidence. I changed the cutoffs from 5 and 10 percent to 2 and 3, to better display the split between such a small number of counties.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 5 × 6
  GEOID NAME                            myvarE myvarM   popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                            <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 44001 Bristol County, Rhode Island     22071    703  50568    NA
2 44003 Kent County, Rhode Island        79144   1590 170658    NA
3 44005 Newport County, Rhode Island     37266    948  85095    NA
4 44007 Providence County, Rhode Island 285849   4075 658977    NA
5 44009 Washington County, Rhode Island  57178   1424 130073    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 2  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 3 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence          1        658977 
2 Low confidence           1         50568 
3 Moderate                 3        128609.


The average population of the single high confidence county is 658,977. The lowest confidence county has the lowest average population, at 50,568. Confidence increases alongside an increase in average population.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
We know the most about commuter population from counties with higher populations, like Providence County. We know the least about Bristol County, which is roughly thirteen times smaller in population than Providence County. This makes sense, as smaller places in population have a smaller sample size, and thus a larger margin of error. A smaller population means less data points, and a result, a higher sense of uncertainty. If a state agency allocated funding based on my commuter variable, the areas with less confidence would likely be hurt, since there are uncertainties: what if they allocate an insufficient amount of dollars for a project, based on too low of an estimate of commuters? The moderate confidence level contains three out of the five of the state’s counties. These contain a range of populations, and we could only be so “certain” about them. But Providence County with a 1.45% margin of error, which contains the state’s capital, has the highest reliability: we could be confident in funding a roadworks project, based on an estimate of how many commuters’ lives it may improve. On the flip side, counties with lower reliability might even miss out on funding or projects, if the state agency is less certain of a quantifiable benefit.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
This is not a competition. There’s no leaderboard and no target RMSE. The goal is to practice the full prediction workflow on a question you choose, and to find out what actually helps. Some features you’re sure will help won’t, and some you add on a whim will. Both are findings.
You’ll:

Choose a tract-level outcome for Philadelphia and check whether it’s reliable enough to model (Weeks 2–3).
Fit a baseline model and cross-validate it (Week 5).
Pull data from Philadelphia’s open data portal through its API and build spatial features: counts, densities, and distances (Week 4, plus one new tool).
Transform variables with logs, squared terms, and categories. Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before Part 5.
Keep a model log the whole way through, and compare where your first and final models go wrong.

Timing. Parts 1–4 use only what we’ve covered through Week 5. You can finish them before the October 9 lecture. Part 5 is new material; the lecture explains it, and the instructions below give you the essentials.
Type the code yourself. The worked examples show the pattern. Your job is to apply it to your outcome and your data choices.








Important1. Don’t drop rows



Every model is cross-validated on the same tracts with the same folds, so the rows in your model log are comparable. If a new variable has missing values, fill them (for example, 0 for a count, or the median with a note) or choose a different variable. The cv_rmse() helper below will stop and tell you if you break this rule.


Your outcome comes from the 2019–2023 ACS. Pull open data from 2023 or earlier (2021–2023 is ideal). Using 2025 data to predict a 2023 outcome uses information from the future, which a real prediction model would never have.



Don’t use any variable that’s built from your outcome or measures the same thing another way. Ask yourself: would an agency trying to predict this outcome for a tract have this variable? If the answer is “only because it’s basically the outcome,” leave it out.

text:
Part 0: Setup


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(caret)

Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != ""   # should print TRUE


[1] TRUE



The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}




The model log
Every time you fit a new model, add a row. By the end, this table is the story of your assignment.


Code
model_log <- tibble(
  model   = character(),
  added   = character(),
  cv_rmse = numeric(),
  notes   = character()
)

section: Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:


Code
# What kinds of crime are in the incidents table in 2023?

                         WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01' AND dispatch_date < '2024-01-01'

Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.

log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.

5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.

5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.

tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(ring)
m_cat <- lm(y ~ ring, data = tracts) summary(m_cat)

**Reading the coefficients:** R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the **reference level** (here, "Core," the first level). Each coefficient is the **difference from the reference**: `ringOuter` is how much higher or lower predicted Y is in outer tracts *compared to core tracts*, holding everything else in the model constant. To change the reference, use `relevel(ring, ref = "Outer")`.

::: {.callout-note}
## Check your group sizes
If a category has only a handful of tracts, its coefficient is unstable, and in cross-validation some folds may not contain it at all. Aim for at least 20 tracts per category.

The scenario
The Georgia Department of Community Supervision is considering a risk model to guide parole decisions. Every person released to parole would get a predicted probability of being rearrested within three years. The department has two proposed uses:

Use A: people above a threshold get more restrictive supervision (more check-ins, electronic monitoring, faster revocation).
Use B: people above a threshold get priority for reentry services (housing assistance, job placement, a case manager).

The department has promised that the model will not use race. You’ve been hired to build it and to tell them whether that promise means what they think it means.

Part 7: The memo
Dear Deputy Commissioner,This model gives each person leaving prison a risk score. We pick a cutoff, and everyone above it is labeled “high risk.” The right cutoff depends on what the label triggers. I tested the model on about 7,800 people it had not seen before. Given one person who was rearrested and one who wasn’t, it scores the rearrested person higher about 71% of the time. It’s better than a coin flip, but far from reliable. About 57% of people in the data were rearrested within three years, so the default cutoff of 0.5 labels about 70% of people high risk, which is too many to be useful.
Use A (more restrictive supervision): cutoff of 0.60. For someone wrongly flagged, a false positive means extra check-ins, monitoring, and a higher chance of being sent back for a technical violation, all for a person who would not have been rearrested. That harms the person and costs the state money. A false negative means someone who is rearrested was supervised normally, which is a real cost but one the model cannot prevent reliably. So I am in favor of fewer false alarms. At 0.60, the model still wrongly flags about 40% of Black and 31% of white parolees who were not rearrested, and it misses about a third of those who were. Because those errors remain high, the score should never trigger restrictions on its own.
Use B (priority for reentry services): cutoff of 0.40. A false positive here means someone who didn’t need help is offered housing or job support, which is a modest cost and arguably a benefit. A false negative means someone who needed support is overlooked. So I favor catching more people. At 0.40, the model reaches about 92% of Black and 89% of white parolees who were later rearrested. The drawback is that it flags most people (roughly three in four of those not rearrested), so the Department needs capacity to serve them or a way to rank who goes first.
Does “the model doesn’t use race” mean it treats Black and white parolees the same? No. At 0.5, the model labeled 73% of Black parolees high risk versus 66% of white parolees, though actual rearrest rates were close (58% and 56%). Among people who were not rearrested, 58% of Black parolees were wrongly flagged versus 49% of white parolees. The gap held at every cutoff I tested, with Black parolees wrongly flagged about 1.2 to 1.3 times as often. A likely reason is age: Black parolees in this data are younger at release (33% were 27 or under, versus 21% of white parolees), and youth strongly raises the score. In addition, wrongly flagged people were somewhat more common in areas with more Black parolees. Leaving race out of the formula means race is not an input, not that outcomes are equal.
In Use A, the unequal errors fall on Black parolees as extra restriction. In Use B, they come as extra offers of help, which is a much smaller concern. I would not deploy this for Use A, unless the Department can show the gap in wrongly flagged Black and white parolees has been closed or justified, and a person reviews every flag with authority to override it.
